questions.prompt: What is the chapter's central rule for choosing a lifestyle?

options.text: Indoor-only is always correct because it removes every meaningful welfare risk.
options.feedback: Indoor-only reduces some risks but requires full environmental provision and is not universally correct for every cat and household.

options.text: Match the cat's temperament and history with the household's real setting, risks, and capacity.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The position statement treats every lifestyle as a risk-benefit decision for the individual case.

options.text: Outdoor access is always better because it lets cats express natural behaviour without human design.
options.feedback: Outdoor access also carries significant safety risks and does not remove the need for deliberate care or controlled planning.

questions.prompt: What does an indoor-only decision commit the household to?

options.text: A closed door plus food and one litter box, because outside risk is the main welfare issue.
options.feedback: A closed door is not enough. The indoor environment must deliberately meet resting, toileting, play, foraging, territory, social, and scent needs.

options.text: Implementing the full environmental-needs pillars and checking that they continue to work for this cat.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Indoor-only is a complete environmental-care commitment, not the absence of an outdoor plan.

options.text: Replacing all hunting and play opportunities with larger meals so the cat feels satisfied.
options.feedback: A full bowl does not replace predatory sequence or foraging opportunities and may create a different preventive-health concern.

questions.prompt: Which option accurately describes controlled outdoor access?

options.text: A secure enclosure, cat-safe fencing, or gradually trained harness-and-leash use.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. These methods create a managed middle ground between indoor-only life and unrestricted roaming.

options.text: Any balcony or garden visit counts as controlled when a person is somewhere nearby.
options.feedback: Supervision does not make an unsecured physical setting safe. Escape routes, edges, traffic, and actual containment still matter.

options.text: Free-roaming during daylight is controlled because nighttime is the only risky period.
options.feedback: Nighttime confinement is one recommendation, not proof that unrestricted daytime roaming is controlled or low-risk.

questions.prompt: Which recommendation applies regardless of the final lifestyle?

options.text: Microchipping plus visible identification.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Identification remains relevant for indoor cats, controlled-access cats, and managed outdoor arrangements.

options.text: Harness training, even when the cat consistently shows fear around the equipment.
options.feedback: Harness access is optional and must remain gradual and consent-aware. Repeated fear can mean the method or plan does not fit.

options.text: Nighttime outdoor confinement in a barn or colony setting.
options.feedback: That arrangement is relevant only in narrow circumstances and does not describe every cat or Milo's own situation.

questions.prompt: Milo is confident, lives by a busy street, and can visit a secure garden on weekends. Which plan is best supported?

options.text: Keep the indoor pillars complete and try gradual harness training for supervised garden visits, with ID either way.
options.feedback: This is the best answer because it combines ordinary indoor welfare, a genuinely controlled option, gradual training, and universal identification.

options.text: Let her use the open balcony because frequent supervision offsets the street and fall risks.
options.feedback: An unenclosed balcony remains physically uncontrolled. Being present does not reliably prevent escape or a sudden accident.

options.text: Rule out all outdoor experience forever because the primary home has no yard.
options.feedback: The secure weekend setting is relevant. The final choice should still depend on Milo's training response and the household's ability to manage it.

questions.prompt: A former outdoor-only barn cat remains distressed after a genuinely complete indoor setup. What is the responsible response?

options.text: Continue indoor-only indefinitely because a complete pillar setup must suit every cat eventually.
options.feedback: This applies a generally responsible plan too rigidly and ignores the cat's history and persistent evidence that the fit remains poor.

options.text: Reconsider a secure or managed outdoor arrangement without treating unrestricted release as the only alternative.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. It keeps the narrow exception narrow and retains safety and management within the reconsideration.

options.text: Open the door without management because indoor enrichment has already been tried.
options.feedback: Failure of one arrangement does not justify unmanaged risk. The source describes managed alternatives rather than uncontrolled release.

questions.prompt: Milo repeatedly freezes and withdraws during gradual harness contact but remains settled indoors. What should change?

options.text: Force a brief outdoor trial because the new environment may overcome equipment fear.
options.feedback: Forcing the next stage breaks the no-force training method and gives Milo less control when her current signals already request distance.

options.text: Pause, keep indoor needs fully met, and reassess pace or whether controlled outdoor access fits Milo at all.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis. The lifestyle process remains responsive to temperament evidence rather than committed to a predetermined outcome.

options.text: Remove the harness and allow free-roaming because only the equipment has been shown to be unpleasant.
options.feedback: Harness avoidance does not prove unrestricted outdoor access is desired or safe. That conclusion outruns the observed evidence.
